chapter_title: Organic Chemistry Name Reactions: Complete Exam & Mechanism Guide

notes_list.title: What is a Name Reaction?
notes_list.basic_overview: A name reaction is an organic transformation traditionally associated with a particular chemist or commonly recognized name. For examinations, the reaction name must be connected with substrate, reagent, conditions, major product and mechanism.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Exam rule: Do not memorize only the reagent. Build the chain: substrate class → reagent/condition → reaction type → product → mechanism → selectivity. Example: Aldehyde/ketone + Zn(Hg)/HCl → hydrocarbon is Clemmensen reduction, whereas aldehyde/ketone + NH2NH2/KOH, heat → hydrocarbon is Wolff–Kishner reduction.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The source describes the transformation as: A name reaction is an organic transformation traditionally associated with a particular chemist or commonly recognized name. For examinations, the reaction name must be connected with substrate, reagent, conditions, major product and mechanism. The mechanism should be read as activation of the stated substrate, formation of the key reactive intermediate, the bond-making/bond-breaking event described by the reaction, and the stated work-up/product-forming step.

1. Activate the stated substrate with the listed reagent/conditions.
2. Generate the key reactive intermediate or electrophile/nucleophile implied by the reaction.
3. Carry out the characteristic bond-forming, bond-breaking or rearrangement step.
4. Complete proton transfer/work-up and verify the characteristic product.

notes_list.basic_overview: For every named reaction identify the starting functional group, key reagent, bond-forming or bond-breaking event and characteristic product.
notes_list.extra_info_content:

notes_list.title: Name Reaction vs Named Reagent
notes_list.basic_overview: A named reagent and a name reaction are not identical. A reagent may participate in several transformations, while a name reaction describes a characteristic transformation.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Example: PCC is a named reagent used for oxidation, but PCC oxidation itself is not always treated as a single universally defined name reaction. In contrast, Cannizzaro, Aldol, Claisen and Diels–Alder describe characteristic reaction patterns.

notes_list.title: Aldol Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes or ketones containing an alpha-hydrogen can undergo base- or acid-catalysed condensation to form a beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound, which may dehydrate to an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Example: 2 CH3CHO --dilute NaOH→ CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO; on heating/dehydration → CH3CH=CHCHO. Mechanistically, base generates an enolate, the enolate attacks another carbonyl compound, protonation gives the beta-hydroxy product and dehydration gives the conjugated alkene. Exam trap: aldehydes/ketones without alpha-H cannot undergo the normal self-aldol pathway.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Base removes an alpha-hydrogen to form an enolate. The enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second aldehyde/ketone, giving an alkoxide. Protonation gives the beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound; heating can promote dehydration to the conjugated alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl.

1. Generate the enolate at the alpha-carbon.
2. Form the new C–C bond by enolate attack on a second carbonyl.
3. Protonate the alkoxide to give the beta-hydroxy product.
4. If heated/acid or base catalysis permits, eliminate water to form the conjugated alkene.

notes_list.title: Crossed Aldol Condensation
notes_list.basic_overview: A crossed aldol reaction occurs between two different carbonyl compounds. Selectivity is easier when one partner forms the nucleophilic enolate while the other partner lacks alpha-hydrogen.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Benzaldehyde lacks alpha-H and therefore commonly acts as the electrophilic carbonyl partner in crossed aldol reactions with acetone or acetophenone derivatives. Multiple products may occur when both reactants possess alpha-H.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
One carbonyl partner is converted to an enolate while the other acts as the electrophile. The enolate forms a C–C bond at the second carbonyl, followed by protonation and, when appropriate, dehydration.

1. Identify the controlled enolate donor.
2. Generate its enolate.
3. Attack the electrophilic carbonyl partner.
4. Protonate and dehydrate when the reaction conditions favor condensation.

notes_list.title: Claisen Condensation
notes_list.basic_overview: An ester containing an alpha-hydrogen reacts with a suitable alkoxide base to form a beta-keto ester through carbon–carbon bond formation.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
General pattern: 2 RCH2COOR' --RO−/ROH→ RCOCH2CH2COOR' followed by formation of the beta-keto ester framework. The alkoxide base is generally chosen to match the ester alkoxy group to minimize transesterification. A final acidic work-up protonates the enolate.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Alkoxide removes an alpha-hydrogen from an ester to form an ester enolate. The enolate attacks a second ester carbonyl; tetrahedral collapse expels alkoxide and gives a beta-keto ester enolate. Acidic work-up protonates the enolate.

1. Form the ester enolate with a matching alkoxide base.
2. Attack the second ester carbonyl.
3. Collapse the tetrahedral intermediate and expel alkoxide.
4. Acidic work-up protonates the beta-keto ester enolate.

notes_list.title: Dieckmann Condensation
notes_list.basic_overview: Dieckmann condensation is the intramolecular version of the Claisen condensation and commonly produces cyclic beta-keto esters.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The reaction is especially favorable for formation of five- and six-membered rings. Exam strategy: identify a diester containing an alpha-H and check whether intramolecular attack can create a favorable ring.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
An intramolecular ester enolate attacks another ester group in the same molecule. Tetrahedral collapse forms a cyclic beta-keto ester enolate, which is protonated on work-up.

1. Deprotonate the suitable alpha-carbon.
2. Intramolecularly attack the second ester carbonyl.
3. Eliminate alkoxide and close the ring.
4. Protonate the cyclic beta-keto ester enolate.

notes_list.title: Perkin Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: An aromatic aldehyde reacts with an acid anhydride in the presence of the corresponding carboxylate base to produce an alpha,beta-unsaturated aromatic carboxylic acid after work-up.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Classical example: benzaldehyde + acetic anhydride/sodium acetate → cinnamic acid after hydrolysis. The anhydride-derived enolate attacks the aromatic aldehyde followed by elimination and hydrolysis.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The carboxylate base generates an enolate from the acid anhydride. The enolate adds to the aromatic aldehyde, followed by elimination and hydrolysis to the alpha,beta-unsaturated aromatic acid.

1. Generate the anhydride enolate.
2. Add to the aromatic aldehyde.
3. Eliminate to establish the C=C bond.
4. Hydrolyse the anhydride-derived product to the carboxylic acid.

notes_list.title: Knoevenagel Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes or ketones react with active methylene compounds such as malonates, malononitrile or beta-dicarbonyl compounds under basic or amine catalysis to form alkenes.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The active methylene compound is sufficiently acidic because its conjugate base is stabilized by electron-withdrawing groups. The reaction commonly gives a conjugated alkene. Exam clue: carbonyl + CH2 flanked by strong electron-withdrawing groups.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
A base or amine catalyst removes an acidic methylene proton from an active-methylene compound. The resulting stabilized carbanion adds to the carbonyl compound, followed by dehydration to the alkene.

1. Deprotonate the active methylene group.
2. Add the stabilized carbanion to the carbonyl carbon.
3. Form the beta-hydroxy intermediate.
4. Eliminate water to give the conjugated alkene.

notes_list.title: Benzoin Condensation
notes_list.basic_overview: Two aromatic aldehydes can undergo coupling to form an alpha-hydroxy ketone known as benzoin. Cyanide ion or thiamine-derived catalysts can facilitate the transformation.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Classical reaction: 2 PhCHO --CN−→ PhCH(OH)COPh. Cyanide acts through polarity reversal (umpolung) of the aldehyde carbonyl carbon, allowing carbon–carbon bond formation between two aldehyde molecules.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Cyanide or a thiamine-derived catalyst enables polarity reversal of an aldehyde carbonyl. The activated aldehyde adds to another aldehyde, followed by proton transfers and release of the catalyst to give an alpha-hydroxy ketone.

1. Activate the aldehyde through catalyst addition.
2. Generate the umpolung nucleophilic carbon.
3. Attack a second aldehyde and form the C–C bond.
4. Proton-transfer/catalyst-release steps regenerate the catalyst and give benzoin.

notes_list.title: Grignard Addition
notes_list.basic_overview: Grignard reagents RMgX behave as carbon nucleophiles and add to aldehydes and ketones. Acidic work-up converts the resulting alkoxide into an alcohol.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
RMgX + formaldehyde → primary alcohol; RMgX + aldehyde other than formaldehyde → secondary alcohol; RMgX + ketone → tertiary alcohol. Water, alcohols, acids and other proton donors destroy Grignard reagents, so reactions require dry ether or THF-type conditions.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The C–Mg bond of RMgX is strongly polarized toward carbon. Carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon to form an alkoxide, which is protonated during acidic work-up.

1. Treat the carbonyl compound with RMgX under dry conditions.
2. Carbon nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon.
3. Form the tetrahedral magnesium alkoxide.
4. Acidic work-up protonates the alkoxide to the alcohol.

notes_list.title: Grignard with Esters
notes_list.basic_overview: Esters generally react with two equivalents of Grignard reagent to give tertiary alcohols after hydrolysis.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
First addition gives a tetrahedral intermediate followed by loss of alkoxide and formation of a ketone. The ketone reacts rapidly with a second equivalent of Grignard reagent, ultimately giving a tertiary alcohol.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The Grignard reagent adds to the ester and the tetrahedral intermediate expels alkoxide to form a ketone. A second equivalent of Grignard reagent adds to the ketone; work-up gives the tertiary alcohol.

1. First Grignard addition to the ester carbonyl.
2. Collapse with loss of alkoxide to form a ketone.
3. Second Grignard addition to the ketone.
4. Acidic work-up gives the tertiary alcohol.

notes_list.title: Wittig Olefination
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes or ketones react with phosphorus ylides to replace the carbonyl oxygen with a carbon substituent and form an alkene.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
General transformation: R2C=O + Ph3P=CHR → R2C=CHR + Ph3P=O. The strong formation of P=O drives the reaction. Exam clue: carbonyl compound + phosphonium ylide → alkene.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The phosphonium ylide carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon. A betaine/oxaphosphetane pathway leads to cleavage of the C–O/P–C framework and formation of the alkene plus triphenylphosphine oxide.

1. Generate the phosphorus ylide.
2. Add the ylide carbon to the carbonyl carbon.
3. Form the oxaphosphetane-type intermediate.
4. Collapse to the alkene and Ph3P=O.

notes_list.title: Corey–Fuchs Homologation
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes can be converted into terminal alkynes through conversion to a gem-dibromoalkene followed by organolithium-mediated transformation.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Typical sequence: aldehyde → gem-dibromoalkene using CBr4/PPh3-type conditions → terminal alkyne using strong base such as n-BuLi. The reaction is useful for extending carbon skeletons with an alkyne terminus.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The aldehyde is converted to a gem-dibromoalkene. Strong base performs dehydrohalogenation and metalation; the resulting species undergoes further elimination/work-up to the terminal alkyne.

1. Convert the aldehyde to the gem-dibromoalkene.
2. Remove HBr with strong base.
3. Generate the metalated dibromoalkene intermediate.
4. Eliminate the remaining bromide to furnish the terminal alkyne.

notes_list.title: Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl or vinyl halides/triflates react with organoboron compounds in the presence of a palladium catalyst and base to form C–C bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
General pattern: Ar–X + Ar'–B(OH)2 --Pd/base→ Ar–Ar'. The catalytic cycle involves oxidative addition, transmetalation and reductive elimination. Suzuki coupling is valued for functional-group tolerance and the relatively convenient handling of organoboron reagents.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The Pd catalyst undergoes oxidative addition into the aryl/vinyl C–X bond. The organoboron partner transfers its organic group during transmetalation; reductive elimination forms the new C–C bond.

1. Oxidative addition of Ar–X to Pd.
2. Base-assisted transmetalation from Ar′–B(OH)2.
3. Form the Pd complex bearing both carbon groups.
4. Reductive elimination gives Ar–Ar′ and regenerates Pd(0).

notes_list.title: Mizoroki–Heck Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: An aryl or vinyl halide reacts with an alkene under palladium catalysis and base to form a substituted alkene.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Key catalytic steps include oxidative addition of the aryl halide, alkene coordination and migratory insertion, beta-hydride elimination and catalyst regeneration. Regioselectivity often favors the more substituted alkene arrangement, but substrate and catalyst conditions matter.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Pd inserts into the aryl/vinyl halide bond, coordinates the alkene and undergoes migratory insertion. Beta-hydride elimination creates the substituted alkene, followed by base-assisted catalyst regeneration.

1. Oxidative addition of the aryl/vinyl halide to Pd.
2. Alkene coordination and migratory insertion.
3. Beta-hydride elimination to form the substituted alkene.
4. Base-assisted regeneration of the active Pd catalyst.

notes_list.title: Sonogashira Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl or vinyl halides react with terminal alkynes under palladium catalysis, often with a copper co-catalyst or copper-free variants, to form C(sp2)–C(sp) bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Exam clue: aryl halide + terminal alkyne + Pd catalyst → aryl alkyne. The terminal alkyne is deprotonated and transferred to the palladium catalytic system before reductive elimination.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Pd activates the aryl/vinyl halide while the terminal alkyne is converted into a metal acetylide. Transmetalation and reductive elimination form the C(sp2)–C(sp) bond.

1. Oxidative addition of Ar–X to Pd.
2. Generate the terminal-alkyne acetylide.
3. Transfer the acetylide to Pd.
4. Reductive elimination gives Ar–C≡C–R.

notes_list.title: Negishi Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Organozinc reagents couple with organic halides or related electrophiles under transition-metal catalysis to form carbon–carbon bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The organozinc reagent participates in transmetalation after oxidative addition of the electrophile to the metal catalyst, followed by reductive elimination.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Pd/Ni oxidative addition activates the organic halide. The organozinc reagent undergoes transmetalation, placing both carbon groups on the metal; reductive elimination forms the C–C bond.

1. Oxidative addition of the electrophile.
2. Transmetalation from the organozinc reagent.
3. Form the diaryl/alkyl-metal intermediate.
4. Reductive elimination gives the coupled product.

notes_list.title: Kumada Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Grignard reagents react with aryl or vinyl halides under nickel or palladium catalysis to form carbon–carbon bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Exam clue: organomagnesium reagent + aryl/vinyl halide + Ni/Pd → coupled product. Grignard reagents are highly reactive, so functional-group compatibility can be lower than with milder organoboron reagents.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The organic halide undergoes oxidative addition to Pd/Ni. A Grignard reagent transfers its organic group to the metal; reductive elimination forms the new C–C bond.

1. Oxidative addition of Ar/Vinyl–X.
2. Transmetalation from RMgX.
3. Arrange both carbon groups on the metal center.
4. Reductive elimination gives the coupled product.

notes_list.title: Baeyer–Villiger Oxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: Ketones are converted into esters using peroxy acids or related oxidants. Cyclic ketones give lactones.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The oxygen inserted between carbonyl carbon and one substituent. Migratory aptitude is important: groups with greater ability to stabilize positive charge generally migrate more readily. Aldehydes can give formate-related products under suitable conditions.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
A peroxy acid adds to the ketone carbonyl to form a Criegee-type intermediate. One adjacent group migrates to oxygen as the O–O bond cleaves, producing an ester/lactone.

1. Protonate/activate the carbonyl and add the peroxy acid.
2. Form the tetrahedral peroxide intermediate.
3. Migrate one carbon group from carbonyl carbon to oxygen while O–O cleavage occurs.
4. Deprotonate to give the ester or lactone.

notes_list.title: OsO4 Dihydroxylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkenes can be converted into vicinal cis-diols through osmium tetroxide-mediated syn dihydroxylation.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
OsO4 adds to both alkene carbons from the same face, leading to syn addition. Catalytic OsO4 can be regenerated using a co-oxidant such as NMO or H2O2.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The source describes the transformation as: Alkenes can be converted into vicinal cis-diols through osmium tetroxide-mediated syn dihydroxylation. The mechanism should be read as activation of the stated substrate, formation of the key reactive intermediate, the bond-making/bond-breaking event described by the reaction, and the stated work-up/product-forming step.

1. Activate the stated substrate with the listed reagent/conditions.
2. Generate the key reactive intermediate or electrophile/nucleophile implied by the reaction.
3. Carry out the characteristic bond-forming, bond-breaking or rearrangement step.
4. Complete proton transfer/work-up and verify the characteristic product.

notes_list.title: Clemmensen Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to hydrocarbons using zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid under strongly acidic conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
General transformation: R2C=O → R2CH2. Key exam distinction: Clemmensen is strongly acidic, whereas Wolff–Kishner reduction is strongly basic. Choose based on whether the molecule is stable under acidic or basic conditions.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Under strongly acidic conditions, the carbonyl group is converted to a zinc-associated intermediate and ultimately reduced to a methylene group.

1. Activate the carbonyl under strongly acidic conditions.
2. Interact the carbonyl with Zn/Hg at the metal surface.
3. Transfer hydrogen/electron equivalents to the carbonyl carbon.
4. Replace C=O by CH2 after the reduction sequence.

notes_list.title: Wolff–Kishner Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes and ketones are converted into hydrocarbons through hydrazone formation followed by strongly basic heating.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Typical conditions involve hydrazine or a substituted hydrazine and strong base such as KOH with heat. Exam comparison: Clemmensen = acidic; Wolff–Kishner = basic.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The carbonyl first condenses with hydrazine to form a hydrazone. Strong base deprotonates the hydrazone; successive proton/electron rearrangements expel nitrogen and generate the hydrocarbon.

1. Form the hydrazone from carbonyl + NH2NH2.
2. Deprotonate under strongly basic conditions.
3. Transfer protons/electrons through the hydrazone and expel N2.
4. Protonate the resulting carbanion to give the hydrocarbon.

notes_list.title: Birch Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aromatic rings are partially reduced to nonconjugated or cyclohexadiene-type products using an alkali metal, liquid ammonia and an alcohol proton source.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The reaction produces a 1,4-diene system. Substituent effects influence which carbon atoms retain the double bonds. Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing substituents affect regiochemistry differently, making substituent analysis important for advanced exam problems.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
An aromatic ring receives an electron from an alkali metal, is protonated by an alcohol, receives a second electron and is protonated again. Substituent effects control which carbon atoms retain the double bonds.

1. Single-electron transfer to the aromatic ring.
2. Protonate the radical anion.
3. Second electron transfer and protonation.
4. Obtain the 1,4-dihydroaromatic product with substituent-dependent regiochemistry.

notes_list.title: Luche Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Sodium borohydride in the presence of cerium(III) salts, commonly CeCl3, provides enhanced selective reduction of carbonyl compounds, especially aldehydes and ketones in suitable systems.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
A common exam concept is chemoselectivity: NaBH4/CeCl3 can favor carbonyl reduction while avoiding some competing reactions that stronger hydride reagents might cause.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The source describes the transformation as: Sodium borohydride in the presence of cerium(III) salts, commonly CeCl3, provides enhanced selective reduction of carbonyl compounds, especially aldehydes and ketones in suitable systems. The mechanism should be read as activation of the stated substrate, formation of the key reactive intermediate, the bond-making/bond-breaking event described by the reaction, and the stated work-up/product-forming step.

1. Activate the stated substrate with the listed reagent/conditions.
2. Generate the key reactive intermediate or electrophile/nucleophile implied by the reaction.
3. Carry out the characteristic bond-forming, bond-breaking or rearrangement step.
4. Complete proton transfer/work-up and verify the characteristic product.

notes_list.title: Rosenmund Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Acid chlorides are selectively reduced to aldehydes using hydrogen gas over poisoned palladium catalyst.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Typical catalyst: Pd/BaSO4, often modified or poisoned to reduce over-reduction of the aldehyde. General transformation: RCOCl → RCHO.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The acid chloride adsorbs on poisoned Pd and is hydrogenated to an aldehyde. The poisoned catalyst suppresses further reduction of the aldehyde to the alcohol.

1. Adsorb the acid chloride on Pd/BaSO4.
2. Activate H2 on the catalyst.
3. Reduce the acyl chloride to the aldehyde.
4. Desorb the aldehyde while catalyst poisoning limits over-reduction.

notes_list.title: Friedel–Crafts Alkylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Aromatic rings react with suitable alkylating agents in the presence of Lewis acids such as AlCl3 to introduce an alkyl group.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Classical example: benzene + CH3Cl/AlCl3 → toluene. Limitations include carbocation rearrangements, polyalkylation and failure with strongly deactivated aromatic rings. Friedel–Crafts alkylation is generally unsuitable for strongly electron-withdrawing substituents.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
A Lewis acid activates the alkylating reagent to a carbocation-like electrophile. The aromatic ring attacks to form a sigma complex, followed by deprotonation and catalyst regeneration.

1. Generate the electrophile with Lewis-acid activation.
2. Aromatic pi electrons attack the electrophile.
3. Form the sigma complex.
4. Remove H+ to restore aromaticity.

notes_list.title: Friedel–Crafts Acylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Aromatic rings react with acyl chlorides or acid anhydrides in the presence of Lewis acids to form aryl ketones.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The electrophile is an acylium ion, RCO+. Because the acylium ion is resonance stabilized, rearrangement is normally avoided. Acylation usually stops after monoacylation because the acyl group deactivates the ring.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
AlCl3 generates the resonance-stabilized acylium ion. Benzene attacks the acylium ion to form a sigma complex; deprotonation restores aromaticity and work-up releases the aryl ketone.

1. Generate RCO+ from the acyl chloride/AlCl3 system.
2. Aromatic ring attacks the acylium ion.
3. Form the sigma complex and remove H+.
4. Aqueous work-up releases the aryl ketone.

notes_list.title: Reimer–Tiemann Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Phenols can be converted into mainly ortho-hydroxy aromatic aldehydes using chloroform and strong base.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The reaction generates dichlorocarbene from CHCl3 under strongly basic conditions. Phenoxide directs electrophilic substitution predominantly to the ortho position. Salicylaldehyde is a classical major product from phenol.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Base converts CHCl3 to dichlorocarbene. Phenoxide activates the aromatic ring toward electrophilic substitution, and the carbene-derived group is installed predominantly ortho; hydrolysis gives the aldehyde.

1. Generate dichlorocarbene from CHCl3/base.
2. Form phenoxide from phenol.
3. Electrophilic substitution installs the –CHCl2-derived group, mainly ortho.
4. Hydrolyse to the –CHO group.

notes_list.title: Gattermann Formylation
notes_list.basic_overview: Aromatic diazonium salts can be converted into aromatic aldehydes under conditions involving HCN/HCl and a Lewis-acid catalyst in the classical formylation.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Do not confuse Gattermann formylation of diazonium compounds with Gattermann–Koch formylation of aromatic hydrocarbons using CO/HCl.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The source describes the transformation as: Aromatic diazonium salts can be converted into aromatic aldehydes under conditions involving HCN/HCl and a Lewis-acid catalyst in the classical formylation. The mechanism should be read as activation of the stated substrate, formation of the key reactive intermediate, the bond-making/bond-breaking event described by the reaction, and the stated work-up/product-forming step.

1. Activate the stated substrate with the listed reagent/conditions.
2. Generate the key reactive intermediate or electrophile/nucleophile implied by the reaction.
3. Carry out the characteristic bond-forming, bond-breaking or rearrangement step.
4. Complete proton transfer/work-up and verify the characteristic product.

notes_list.title: Pinacol–Pinacolone Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Vicinal diols undergo acid-catalysed rearrangement to carbonyl compounds through loss of water followed by migration.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The reaction involves protonation of an OH group, water loss, carbocation formation and 1,2-migration with carbonyl formation. Migratory aptitude and carbocation stability influence product formation.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Acid protonates one hydroxyl group and water leaves to give a carbocation. A neighboring group migrates as the second oxygen forms the carbonyl, followed by deprotonation.

1. Protonate the leaving OH group.
2. Eliminate water to form a carbocation.
3. Perform 1,2-migration while the adjacent OH forms C=O.
4. Deprotonate to give the carbonyl product.

notes_list.title: Cumene Process
notes_list.basic_overview: Cumene is oxidized to cumene hydroperoxide, which undergoes acid-catalysed cleavage to produce phenol and acetone.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Industrial significance: benzene + propene → cumene; oxidation → cumene hydroperoxide; acid cleavage → phenol + acetone. Exam clue: major industrial route to phenol.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Cumene is oxidized by air to cumene hydroperoxide. Acid-catalysed cleavage/rearrangement produces phenol and acetone.

1. Alkylate benzene to cumene.
2. Oxidize the benzylic position to cumene hydroperoxide.
3. Acidically cleave/rearrange the hydroperoxide.
4. Obtain phenol and acetone.

notes_list.title: Hydroboration–Oxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkenes react with borane or substituted boranes followed by oxidation with hydrogen peroxide under basic conditions to give alcohols with overall anti-Markovnikov hydration.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The H and B atoms add syn across the double bond, with boron generally attaching to the less substituted carbon. Oxidation replaces the C–B bond with C–O without changing the carbon framework. Overall result: anti-Markovnikov alcohol with syn addition in the hydroboration step.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Boron and hydrogen add concertedly across the alkene, with boron preferentially on the less substituted carbon. Oxidation replaces C–B by C–O with retention of the carbon skeleton.

1. Concerted syn addition of B–H across C=C.
2. Place B at the less substituted carbon.
3. Oxidize the C–B bond with H2O2/OH−.
4. Obtain the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

notes_list.title: Oxymercuration–Demercuration
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkenes are converted into Markovnikov alcohols without the carbocation rearrangements characteristic of simple acid-catalysed hydration.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Typical sequence: alkene + Hg(OAc)2/H2O followed by NaBH4. The mercurinium ion intermediate controls regioselectivity, while the final demercuration replaces the C–Hg group with hydrogen.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The alkene forms a bridged mercurinium ion. Water attacks the more substituted carbon, deprotonation gives the organomercurial alcohol, and NaBH4 replaces Hg with H.

1. Form the cyclic mercurinium ion.
2. Water attacks the more substituted carbon.
3. Deprotonate to give the organomercurial alcohol.
4. Demercurate with NaBH4 to form the alcohol.

notes_list.title: Kharasch Effect
notes_list.basic_overview: In the presence of peroxides, HBr can add to an alkene through a radical chain mechanism to give the anti-Markovnikov product.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The peroxide effect is characteristic of HBr in the classical exam context. HCl and HI do not normally give the same useful anti-Markovnikov radical addition because of unfavorable energetics of the propagation steps.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Peroxide initiates a radical chain. Br· adds to the alkene so that the more stable carbon radical is formed; abstraction of H from HBr regenerates Br· and gives the anti-Markovnikov product.

1. Generate Br radicals from peroxide/HBr chemistry.
2. Add Br· to the alkene in the orientation giving the more stable carbon radical.
3. Carbon radical abstracts H from HBr.
4. Regenerate Br· and obtain the anti-Markovnikov bromoalkane.

notes_list.title: Lindlar Catalyst Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkynes are selectively hydrogenated to cis-alkenes using a poisoned palladium catalyst known as Lindlar catalyst.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The catalyst is deliberately deactivated so that hydrogenation stops at the alkene stage. Syn addition of hydrogen gives the cis-alkene. Exam comparison: Lindlar → cis-alkene; dissolving-metal reduction such as Na/NH3(l) → trans-alkene.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Poisoned Pd adsorbs the alkyne and hydrogen. Syn addition on the catalyst surface stops at the alkene because the catalyst is deliberately deactivated.

1. Adsorb the alkyne on poisoned Pd.
2. Add the first hydrogen.
3. Add the second hydrogen syn on the surface.
4. Desorb the cis-alkene before further reduction.

notes_list.title: Na/NH3 Reduction of Alkynes
notes_list.basic_overview: Alkynes are reduced to trans-alkenes under dissolving-metal conditions such as sodium or lithium in liquid ammonia.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The mechanism proceeds through radical-anion and protonation steps, leading to anti addition overall. Exam clue: alkyne → trans-alkene.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
A dissolving metal transfers an electron to the alkyne, followed by protonation. A second electron/proton sequence gives the trans-alkene.

1. Single-electron transfer to the alkyne.
2. Protonation forms a vinyl radical.
3. Second electron transfer gives a vinyl anion.
4. Protonation furnishes the trans-alkene.

notes_list.title: Diels–Alder Cycloaddition
notes_list.basic_overview: A conjugated diene reacts with an alkene or alkyne dienophile through a thermal [4+2] cycloaddition to form a six-membered ring.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The reaction is stereospecific and concerted. The diene generally needs an s-cis conformation. Electron-withdrawing groups on the dienophile usually increase reactivity, while electron-donating groups on the diene can increase reactivity. The endo product is often kinetically favored with suitable substituents.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
A conjugated diene and dienophile undergo a concerted [4+2] cycloaddition through a six-membered transition state, forming two sigma bonds and one new pi bond.

1. Place the diene in the s-cis conformation.
2. Align diene and dienophile orbitals.
3. Make both C–C sigma bonds concertedly.
4. Form the cyclohexene-type product with stereochemical information retained.

notes_list.title: Claisen Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Allyl vinyl ethers undergo a thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement to form gamma,delta-unsaturated carbonyl compounds.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The rearrangement is concerted and proceeds through a six-membered transition-state arrangement. Bond connectivity changes without ionic intermediates. Stereochemical information can be transferred predictably through the cyclic transition state.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
An allyl vinyl ether undergoes a concerted [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement through a six-membered transition state to a gamma,delta-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

1. Adopt a favorable six-membered transition-state geometry.
2. Break the allyl O–C bond while forming the new C–C bond.
3. Shift the pi bonds concertedly.
4. Tautomerization/formation of the carbonyl gives the product.

notes_list.title: Cope Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: A 1,5-diene undergoes a thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement to another 1,5-diene.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The reaction proceeds through a six-membered cyclic transition state. Chair-like transition states are often favored when steric interactions are minimized.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
A 1,5-diene undergoes a concerted [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement through a six-membered transition state to a constitutional isomeric 1,5-diene.

1. Adopt a chair-like six-membered transition state when favorable.
2. Break the sigma bond and form the new sigma bond concertedly.
3. Shift the two pi bonds simultaneously.
4. Obtain the rearranged 1,5-diene.

notes_list.title: Electrocyclic Ring Opening and Closing
notes_list.basic_overview: Conjugated polyenes undergo reversible ring opening or ring closure through electrocyclic reactions whose stereochemical mode depends on the number of pi electrons and thermal or photochemical conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Woodward–Hoffmann rules: under thermal conditions, systems with 4n pi electrons undergo conrotatory electrocyclization, while systems with 4n+2 pi electrons undergo disrotatory electrocyclization. Photochemical conditions reverse these preferences.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The source describes the transformation as: Conjugated polyenes undergo reversible ring opening or ring closure through electrocyclic reactions whose stereochemical mode depends on the number of pi electrons and thermal or photochemical conditions. The mechanism should be read as activation of the stated substrate, formation of the key reactive intermediate, the bond-making/bond-breaking event described by the reaction, and the stated work-up/product-forming step.

1. Activate the stated substrate with the listed reagent/conditions.
2. Generate the key reactive intermediate or electrophile/nucleophile implied by the reaction.
3. Carry out the characteristic bond-forming, bond-breaking or rearrangement step.
4. Complete proton transfer/work-up and verify the characteristic product.

notes_list.title: Beckmann Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Oximes undergo acid-promoted rearrangement to amides. Cyclic ketoximes can produce lactams.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The group anti to the leaving group migrates from carbon to nitrogen as water or another leaving group departs. Therefore stereochemical configuration of the oxime is important. Exam clue: ketoxime → amide; cyclic ketoxime → lactam.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Activation of the oxime OH allows loss of water. The group anti to the leaving group migrates from carbon to nitrogen as the nitrilium ion forms; hydrolysis gives the amide.

1. Convert the oxime OH into a good leaving group.
2. The anti group migrates as water leaves.
3. Form the nitrilium intermediate.
4. Hydrolyse to the amide/lactam.

notes_list.title: Baeyer–Villiger Migratory Aptitude
notes_list.basic_overview: In Baeyer–Villiger oxidation, one group adjacent to the carbonyl migrates to oxygen while the carbonyl compound is converted into an ester or lactone.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Typical migratory aptitude trends depend on substrate and conditions; groups better able to stabilize positive charge in the transition state generally migrate more readily. Hydride and tertiary-type migration can be highly favorable in appropriate substrates.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The key step is migration of a group adjacent to the carbonyl onto oxygen in the peroxide intermediate. The relative ability of groups to stabilize positive charge influences which group migrates.

1. Form the peroxide addition intermediate.
2. Compare the two possible migrating groups.
3. Migrate the favored group to oxygen with O–O cleavage.
4. Form the ester/lactone.

notes_list.title: Favorskii Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Alpha-halo ketones undergo base-induced rearrangement to carboxylic acid derivatives, often producing ring-contracted products when cyclic substrates are used.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The mechanism is commonly described through a cyclopropanone-related intermediate or equivalent pathway depending on substrate and conditions. A key exam clue is alpha-halo ketone + base → rearranged carboxylate/ester/amide derivative.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Base generates a reactive alpha-halo ketone intermediate that undergoes intramolecular rearrangement through a cyclopropanone-related pathway or equivalent mechanism. Nucleophilic attack and ring opening give the rearranged carboxylate derivative.

1. Form the nucleophilic species under basic conditions.
2. Generate the cyclopropanone-related rearrangement intermediate.
3. Nucleophile attacks and ring opening changes the carbon skeleton.
4. Protonation/work-up gives the rearranged acid derivative.

notes_list.title: Hofmann Bromamide Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Primary amides are converted into primary amines containing one fewer carbon atom using bromine and strong base or related hypohalite conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
General transformation: RCONH2 → RNH2 + CO2-derived products. The carbonyl carbon is lost. Mechanistically, the amide is converted into an isocyanate intermediate, which undergoes hydrolysis to the amine.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Hypohalite formation from the primary amide is followed by rearrangement to an isocyanate with loss of the carbonyl carbon. Hydrolysis/decarboxylation of the isocyanate gives the primary amine.

1. Convert the amide to the N-bromoamide.
2. Base promotes rearrangement to the isocyanate.
3. Hydrolyse the isocyanate to a carbamic-acid intermediate.
4. Decarboxylation gives RNH2.

notes_list.title: Curtius Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Acyl azides undergo thermal rearrangement to isocyanates, which can be hydrolysed to primary amines or trapped by alcohols to form carbamates.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
RCO2H can first be converted to an activated derivative and then acyl azide; heating gives RNCO. The migrating group moves from carbonyl carbon to nitrogen during nitrogen extrusion. Like Hofmann rearrangement, the final amine has one fewer carbon than the original carboxylic acid framework.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Heating an acyl azide causes loss of nitrogen and migration of the acyl substituent to nitrogen, forming an isocyanate. The isocyanate can be hydrolysed to an amine or trapped with an alcohol.

1. Heat the acyl azide.
2. Extrude N2 while the R group migrates to nitrogen.
3. Form the isocyanate RNCO.
4. Hydrolyse/trap RNCO to obtain the desired product.

notes_list.title: Schmidt Rearrangement
notes_list.basic_overview: Carboxylic acids and ketones can undergo acid-mediated reactions with hydrazoic acid, giving nitrogen-containing products through migration and nitrogen extrusion.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
For carboxylic acids, the rearrangement can produce isocyanates that lead to amines after hydrolysis. For cyclic ketones, ring-expanded lactams can form.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Under strong acid, hydrazoic acid reacts with the activated carbonyl system. Migration occurs with nitrogen extrusion, producing an isocyanate or ring-expanded lactam precursor depending on substrate.

1. Activate the carbonyl substrate with acid.
2. Add hydrazoic acid/azide to the activated system.
3. Migrate the group with loss of N2.
4. Hydrolyse/trap the resulting isocyanate or rearranged intermediate.

notes_list.title: Cannizzaro Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes without alpha-hydrogen undergo base-induced disproportionation to produce an alcohol and a carboxylate salt.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Example: 2 PhCHO + OH− → PhCH2OH + PhCOO−. One aldehyde molecule is oxidized and another is reduced. Exam clue: non-enolizable aldehyde + concentrated base.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Hydroxide adds to a non-enolizable aldehyde. Hydride transfer from one aldehyde-derived intermediate to another produces an alcohol and a carboxylate.

1. OH− adds to the aldehyde.
2. Form the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.
3. Transfer hydride to a second aldehyde molecule.
4. Proton-transfer gives alcohol and carboxylate.

notes_list.title: Crossed Cannizzaro Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Two different aldehydes without alpha-hydrogen can undergo crossed Cannizzaro reaction, often designed so that one aldehyde acts preferentially as the reducing partner.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Formaldehyde is particularly effective as the aldehyde that is oxidized to formate while another non-enolizable aldehyde is reduced to its alcohol. This selectivity is frequently tested.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Two non-enolizable aldehydes undergo hydride transfer. Formaldehyde is often preferentially oxidized to formate while the other aldehyde is reduced to an alcohol.

1. Hydroxide adds to the aldehyde that will donate hydride.
2. Form the tetrahedral intermediate.
3. Transfer hydride to the second aldehyde.
4. Obtain formate/carboxylate and the corresponding alcohol.

notes_list.title: Haloform Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Methyl ketones and suitable secondary alcohols are oxidatively cleaved under halogen/base conditions to produce carboxylate and haloform.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Iodoform test uses I2/NaOH and gives yellow CHI3 precipitate for methyl ketones and compounds that can be oxidized to methyl ketones, such as ethanol and suitable secondary alcohols containing CH3CH(OH)−.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Base and halogen repeatedly alpha-halogenate a methyl ketone. Hydroxide then attacks the trihalomethyl ketone, and cleavage gives carboxylate plus haloform.

1. Enol/enolate formation allows repeated alpha-halogenation.
2. Convert CH3CO– to C X3CO–.
3. OH− attacks the carbonyl and the tetrahedral intermediate collapses.
4. Produce carboxylate and CHX3.

notes_list.title: Baeyer Test for Unsaturation
notes_list.basic_overview: Cold dilute alkaline potassium permanganate is classically used as a qualitative test for readily oxidizable unsaturation, producing loss of purple permanganate color and formation of manganese dioxide under typical conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
This is a qualitative test rather than a definitive structural proof because other reducing or oxidizable substances can also react with permanganate.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Permanganate oxidizes readily oxidizable C=C/C≡C systems under cold dilute alkaline conditions. The qualitative test is based on reduction of permanganate and formation of manganese dioxide under typical conditions.

1. Alkene/alkyne interacts with permanganate.
2. Oxidation of the unsaturated bond occurs.
3. Mn(VII) is reduced under the test conditions.
4. Loss of purple color and MnO2 formation provide the qualitative observation.

notes_list.title: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Carboxylic acids containing alpha-hydrogen undergo alpha-halogenation using halogen and phosphorus-based reagents, commonly Br2/PBr3-type conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The carboxylic acid is first converted into an acyl halide, which can enolize and undergo alpha-halogenation. Hydrolysis regenerates the carboxylic acid. Exam clue: carboxylic acid + alpha-H → alpha-halo acid.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The carboxylic acid is converted to an acyl halide, which can enolize. Alpha-halogenation occurs at the enol, followed by hydrolysis back to the alpha-halo acid.

1. Convert the carboxylic acid to the acyl halide.
2. Enolize at the alpha-carbon.
3. Halogenate the alpha position.
4. Hydrolyse the acyl halide to regenerate the carboxylic acid.

notes_list.title: Malonic Ester Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Diethyl malonate is deprotonated at the active methylene carbon, alkylated with suitable alkyl halides and then hydrolysed and decarboxylated to synthesize substituted acetic acids.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
General route: CH2(CO2Et)2 → alkylation → hydrolysis → heating/decarboxylation → RCH2CO2H. Primary alkyl halides are generally preferred for clean SN2 alkylation.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The active methylene of diethyl malonate is deprotonated, alkylated by SN2 with a suitable primary electrophile, then hydrolysed and decarboxylated on heating.

1. Form the malonate enolate.
2. Perform SN2 alkylation.
3. Hydrolyse both ester groups.
4. Heat to decarboxylate and obtain the substituted acetic acid.

notes_list.title: Acetoacetic Ester Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Ethyl acetoacetate is alkylated at its active methylene carbon, followed by hydrolysis and decarboxylation to synthesize substituted methyl ketones.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
General sequence: ethyl acetoacetate → enolate formation → alkylation → hydrolysis → decarboxylation → substituted methyl ketone. This is a major retrosynthetic strategy for building ketones.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Ethyl acetoacetate is deprotonated at the active methylene, alkylated, hydrolysed and decarboxylated to give a substituted methyl ketone.

1. Form the acetoacetate enolate.
2. Alkylate by SN2.
3. Hydrolyse the ester.
4. Heat to decarboxylate and form the methyl ketone.

notes_list.title: Arndt–Eistert Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Carboxylic acids can be converted into homologated acids containing one additional carbon through an acid chloride → diazoketone → ketene sequence followed by trapping with water or another nucleophile.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Classical sequence: RCOOH → RCOCl → RCOCHN2 → ketene → RCH2COOH. The carbon count increases by one in the final carboxylic acid.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The carboxylic acid is converted to an acid chloride and then a diazoketone. Wolff-type rearrangement with loss of N2 forms a ketene, which is trapped by water or another nucleophile.

1. Convert RCO2H to RCOCl.
2. Form the diazoketone.
3. Rearrange with loss of N2 to the ketene.
4. Trap the ketene to obtain the one-carbon-homologated acid/derivative.

notes_list.title: Gabriel Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Potassium phthalimide reacts with suitable primary alkyl halides through SN2 substitution and subsequent cleavage gives primary amines.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The method is especially useful for preparing primary amines without the multiple alkylation often associated with direct ammonia alkylation. It is poorly suited to tertiary alkyl halides because SN2 substitution is unfavorable.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Phthalimide nitrogen is deprotonated and attacks a primary alkyl halide by SN2. Cleavage of the N-alkyl phthalimide releases the primary amine.

1. Generate potassium phthalimide.
2. SN2 attack on the primary alkyl electrophile.
3. Cleave the imide derivative by hydrolysis or hydrazinolysis.
4. Release the primary amine.

notes_list.title: Carbylamine Test
notes_list.basic_overview: Primary amines react with chloroform and alcoholic KOH on heating to form isocyanides with a characteristic unpleasant odor.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Only primary amines give the classical carbylamine test. Secondary and tertiary amines do not give this reaction under the standard test conditions. General product: RNH2 → RNC.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Primary amine reacts with dichlorocarbene generated from chloroform/base. The resulting intermediate undergoes conversion to an isocyanide.

1. Generate reactive dichlorocarbene from CHCl3/KOH.
2. Primary amine reacts with the carbene-derived species.
3. Dehydrohalogenation gives the isocyanide.
4. Secondary/tertiary amines do not give the classical test.

notes_list.title: Hofmann Elimination
notes_list.basic_overview: Quaternary ammonium hydroxides undergo elimination on heating to form alkenes. The major alkene is often the less substituted alkene, known as the Hofmann product.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The bulky leaving group and steric factors contribute to preference for abstraction of the most accessible beta-hydrogen. This can oppose the usual Zaitsev orientation observed in many ordinary elimination reactions.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Quaternary ammonium hydroxide undergoes E2-like elimination on heating. Steric effects favor removal of the most accessible beta-hydrogen, often giving the less substituted alkene.

1. Form the quaternary ammonium hydroxide.
2. Heat to promote beta-elimination.
3. Remove the most accessible beta-H while the ammonium group leaves.
4. Form the Hofmann alkene.

notes_list.title: Fischer Indole Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl hydrazines react with aldehydes or ketones under acidic conditions to form indoles.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The carbonyl compound first forms an arylhydrazone, followed by acid-catalysed rearrangement and cyclization to the indole framework. Fischer indole synthesis is one of the most important named methods for constructing indoles.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The arylhydrazine condenses with a carbonyl compound to form a hydrazone. Acid-promoted rearrangement and cyclization construct the indole ring, followed by loss of ammonia/water-equivalent species.

1. Condense arylhydrazine with the aldehyde/ketone.
2. Protonate and rearrange the hydrazone under acid.
3. Cyclize to establish the indole framework.
4. Eliminate/ammonia-related species and rearomatize.

notes_list.title: Paal–Knorr Pyrrole Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: 1,4-dicarbonyl compounds can cyclize to pyrroles under suitable acid-promoted conditions with ammonia or primary amines.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Variants of the Paal–Knorr strategy also provide furans and thiophenes depending on the heteroatom source. Exam clue: 1,4-dicarbonyl → five-membered heterocycle.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
A 1,4-dicarbonyl compound condenses with ammonia/primary amine and cyclizes. Dehydration and aromatization give the pyrrole.

1. Condense the amine with a carbonyl group.
2. Form the second C–N bond by cyclization.
3. Eliminate water.
4. Rearrange/dehydrogenate to the aromatic pyrrole.

notes_list.title: Hantzsch Pyridine Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: Beta-ketoesters, an aldehyde and ammonia or an ammonium source undergo multicomponent condensation to produce substituted 1,4-dihydropyridines, which can be oxidized to pyridines.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The Hantzsch synthesis is a classic multicomponent heterocycle-forming reaction. Oxidation of the dihydropyridine product provides an aromatic pyridine derivative.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Two beta-ketoester units, an aldehyde and ammonia undergo condensation to a 1,4-dihydropyridine. Oxidation then gives the aromatic pyridine derivative.

1. Condense the aldehyde with a beta-ketoester component.
2. Form the second carbon–carbon/carbon–nitrogen bonds through the multicomponent sequence.
3. Cyclize to the 1,4-dihydropyridine.
4. Oxidize to the aromatic pyridine.

notes_list.title: Gewald Thiophene Synthesis
notes_list.basic_overview: A carbonyl compound, an activated nitrile and sulfur undergo base-promoted condensation and cyclization to form substituted 2-aminothiophenes.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Exam clue: carbonyl compound + activated nitrile + sulfur → 2-aminothiophene framework. The reaction is important for medicinal and heterocyclic chemistry.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The carbonyl compound and activated nitrile undergo condensation; sulfur participates in cyclization to form the thiophene ring and the 2-amino substituent.

1. Condense the carbonyl compound with the activated nitrile.
2. Generate the sulfur-reactive intermediate.
3. Cyclize and incorporate sulfur.
4. Rearomatize to the substituted 2-aminothiophene.

notes_list.title: Boc Protection of Amines
notes_list.basic_overview: Amines can be protected as carbamates using di-tert-butyl dicarbonate, commonly written as Boc2O.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Boc protection converts RNH2 into RNHBoc. The Boc group is commonly removed under acidic conditions such as TFA or HCl in suitable solvents. Exam clue: Boc is acid-labile.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The amine attacks one carbonyl of Boc2O, forming a carbamate and releasing tert-butoxide-derived carbonate products. The resulting Boc carbamate is acid-labile.

1. Nucleophilic amine attack on Boc2O.
2. Tetrahedral intermediate collapses with leaving-group departure.
3. Form the Boc carbamate RNHBoc.
4. Acidic conditions can cleave the Boc group.

notes_list.title: Cbz Protection
notes_list.basic_overview: Amines can be protected as carbamates using benzyl chloroformate (Cbz-Cl).
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Cbz-protected amines are commonly deprotected by catalytic hydrogenolysis, for example H2/Pd-C. Exam contrast: Boc is commonly acid-labile, whereas Cbz is commonly removed by hydrogenolysis.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The amine attacks Cbz-Cl and chloride leaves, giving the Cbz carbamate. Hydrogenolysis cleaves the benzyl group to regenerate the amine.

1. Amine attacks the chloroformate carbonyl.
2. Chloride leaves and the carbamate forms.
3. Hydrogenolysis of the benzyl O–CH2Ph bond under H2/Pd-C.
4. Regenerate the free amine.

notes_list.title: Carbonyl Protection as Acetal
notes_list.basic_overview: Aldehydes and ketones can be protected as acetals or ketals by reaction with alcohols under acid catalysis.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Acetal formation is reversible and generally requires removal of water to drive formation. Acetals are stable under many basic conditions and are commonly hydrolysed under aqueous acidic conditions to regenerate the carbonyl.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The carbonyl is protonated and attacked by an alcohol. After hemiacetal formation, a second alcohol adds and water is eliminated to form the acetal.

1. Protonate the carbonyl oxygen.
2. Add the first alcohol to form a hemiacetal.
3. Activate the OH and add the second alcohol.
4. Eliminate water and deprotonate to the acetal.

notes_list.title: THP Protection of Alcohols
notes_list.basic_overview: Alcohols can be protected as tetrahydropyranyl ethers using dihydropyran under acid catalysis.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
THP ethers are commonly stable to many bases and can be removed under acidic hydrolysis conditions. The THP group is useful when a temporary acid-sensitive protection strategy is not appropriate.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The alcohol adds to proton-activated dihydropyran to form a tetrahydropyranyl ether. Acidic hydrolysis reverses the protection.

1. Activate dihydropyran under acid catalysis.
2. Alcohol oxygen attacks the oxocarbenium-like carbon.
3. Proton transfers give the THP ether.
4. Acidic hydrolysis removes the THP group.

notes_list.title: PCC Oxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: Pyridinium chlorochromate commonly oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes and secondary alcohols to ketones under anhydrous conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Exam clue: primary alcohol + PCC → aldehyde under controlled anhydrous conditions. Stronger aqueous chromium(VI) oxidation can continue primary alcohol oxidation to carboxylic acid.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
PCC accepts hydride from an alcohol through chromate ester formation. Elimination gives the aldehyde or ketone while avoiding strongly aqueous over-oxidation in suitable conditions.

1. Form the chromate ester from the alcohol and PCC.
2. Remove the alpha-hydrogen/hydride transfer to chromium.
3. Collapse the ester to the carbonyl compound.
4. Work-up gives aldehyde or ketone.

notes_list.title: DIBAL-H Reduction
notes_list.basic_overview: DIBAL-H can selectively reduce esters and nitriles to aldehydes under controlled low-temperature conditions, although exact selectivity depends on substrate and stoichiometry.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
A common exam transformation is ester → aldehyde using approximately controlled DIBAL-H conditions. Excess or warmer conditions can lead to further reduction.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
DIBAL-H transfers hydride to an ester/nitrile under controlled low-temperature conditions. For suitable esters, a tetrahedral aluminum intermediate can stop at the aldehyde after controlled work-up.

1. Coordinate the carbonyl/functional group to Al.
2. Transfer hydride to form the aluminum-bound intermediate.
3. Controlled reaction/work-up gives the aldehyde for suitable substrates.
4. Excess reagent/warmer conditions can cause further reduction, so stoichiometry and temperature matter.

notes_list.title: mCPBA Epoxidation
notes_list.basic_overview: m-Chloroperoxybenzoic acid is commonly used to convert alkenes into epoxides.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The oxygen transfer is stereospecific: alkene geometry is retained in the relative configuration of substituents in the epoxide. mCPBA can also participate in Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of suitable ketones.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
The alkene reacts with the peracid in a concerted oxygen-transfer step, producing an epoxide and the corresponding carboxylic acid.

1. Alkene approaches the electrophilic peroxy oxygen.
2. Oxygen transfer occurs concertedly.
3. The C=C becomes the three-membered epoxide ring.
4. The peracid is converted to its carboxylic acid.

notes_list.title: NBS Allylic and Benzylic Bromination
notes_list.basic_overview: N-Bromosuccinimide is commonly used as a controlled source of low concentrations of bromine for radical allylic and benzylic bromination.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
NBS maintains a low bromine concentration, favoring radical substitution at allylic or benzylic positions under radical initiation conditions. Exam clue: alkene + NBS/hν → allylic bromination rather than simple addition of Br2.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
NBS maintains a low bromine concentration while radicals abstract allylic/benzylic hydrogen. The resonance-stabilized radical reacts with Br2 to give substitution.

1. Radical initiation generates bromine radicals.
2. Allylic/benzylic H abstraction forms a resonance-stabilized radical.
3. The radical abstracts Br from Br2.
4. NBS regenerates the brominating conditions and the substituted product forms.

notes_list.title: LiAlH4
notes_list.basic_overview: Lithium aluminium hydride is a strong hydride reducing agent capable of reducing many carboxylic acid derivatives, aldehydes and ketones to alcohols or related reduced products.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
LiAlH4 reacts violently with water and protic solvents and is normally used under anhydrous conditions followed by careful work-up. Common exam transformations: carboxylic acid → primary alcohol; ester → primary alcohols; amide → amine.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Aluminium hydride delivers hydride to polar functional groups. Carbonyl derivatives undergo successive hydride transfers and coordination; aqueous work-up protonates the aluminium-bound oxygen or nitrogen products.

1. Coordinate the substrate to aluminium.
2. Transfer hydride to the electrophilic center.
3. Continue hydride transfer where the functional group requires it.
4. Carefully hydrolyse the aluminium complex during work-up.

notes_list.title: NaBH4
notes_list.basic_overview: Sodium borohydride is a milder hydride reagent that commonly reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols under suitable conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Compared with LiAlH4, NaBH4 is generally more chemoselective for aldehydes and ketones and is compatible with many protic solvents under appropriate conditions.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Hydride transfer from borohydride to an electrophilic carbonyl carbon forms an alkoxide. Protonation by solvent/work-up gives the alcohol.

1. Coordinate/approach the carbonyl.
2. Transfer hydride to carbon and push C=O electrons to oxygen.
3. Form the alkoxide intermediate.
4. Protonate to obtain the alcohol.

notes_list.title: Buchwald–Hartwig Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Aryl halides or related electrophiles react with amines under palladium catalysis and suitable ligand/base systems to form aryl amines.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
The catalytic cycle commonly involves oxidative addition, amine coordination/deprotonation, reductive elimination and catalyst regeneration. Ligand choice strongly influences reactivity and selectivity.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Pd catalysis activates the aryl halide, an amine coordinates/deprotonates at the metal, and reductive elimination forms the aryl–N bond.

1. Oxidative addition of Ar–X to Pd.
2. Amine coordination and deprotonation.
3. Form the Pd–N/aryl complex.
4. Reductive elimination gives Ar–NR2.

notes_list.title: Ullmann Reaction
notes_list.basic_overview: Copper-mediated coupling of aryl halides can form biaryls or aryl heteroatom bonds depending on the nucleophile and reaction conditions.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
Classical Ullmann biaryl coupling uses copper and heat. Modern copper-catalysed variants can form C–N, C–O and C–S bonds under more controlled conditions.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Copper catalysis enables coupling of aryl halides with nucleophiles such as amines, phenoxides or thiolates. Transmetalation/ligand exchange and reductive elimination form the aryl–heteroatom bond.

1. Activate the aryl halide at copper.
2. Coordinate the nucleophile.
3. Form the organocopper intermediate.
4. Reductive elimination gives the aryl–heteroatom product.

notes_list.title: Hiyama Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Organosilicon compounds can couple with aryl or vinyl halides under palladium catalysis, often requiring activation by fluoride or base.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
General pattern: organosilane + aryl/vinyl halide → coupled product. The reaction is useful because organosilicon reagents can be relatively stable and convenient to handle.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
An organosilane is activated, commonly by fluoride/base, and transfers its organic group to a Pd catalyst. Coupling with an aryl/vinyl halide gives the C–C product.

1. Oxidative addition of the organic halide to Pd.
2. Activate the organosilane and promote transmetalation.
3. Place both organic groups on Pd.
4. Reductive elimination forms the C–C bond.

notes_list.title: Stille Coupling
notes_list.basic_overview: Organotin reagents couple with organic halides under palladium catalysis to form C–C bonds.
notes_list.extra_info_content:
General pattern: R–SnR3 + Ar–X --Pd→ R–Ar. The reaction is broadly useful but organotin reagent toxicity and waste are important practical disadvantages.

MECHANISM & STEPWISE EXPLANATION
Pd undergoes oxidative addition to the organic halide, then transfers an organic group from the organotin reagent. Reductive elimination forms the coupled product.

1. Oxidative addition of Ar–X to Pd.
2. Transmetalation from R–SnR3.
3. Form the Pd complex bearing both organic groups.
4. Reductive elimination gives the coupled product.
